clue.text: Introduce former husband to model

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse, so former husband gives EX
to model for an artist is to pose

explanation.surface: Someone presents their ex to a fashion model at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To expose someone to an experience is to introduce them to it, a verb sense the clue's opening word shares.

clue.text: At far end of the Bowery vagrant is a minor feature!

indicators.note: the far end of a word is its last letter, here the final letter of the
vagrant means wandering, so the letters of Bowery wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Down at the end of the Bowery in New York, a tramp counts as a small detail.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bowery is a New York street once known for its down-and-outs, so 'vagrant' reads as a tramp, but it is the signal that the street's letters wander, giving YEBROW.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyebrow is a small feature of the face, so a minor feature describes it.

clue.text: An animal, not a vegetable

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letter is taken away

parts.note: the potato is a vegetable
taken as written

explanation.surface: It's a creature, not a plant, the question of animal or vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a vegetable' sounds like the parlour game question but means POTATO without its A.
explanation.definitionFit: The potto is a slow-moving primate of African forests, so it is a kind of animal.

clue.text: Catastrophic mass turn to right after crash

indicators.note: catastrophic suggests a disaster scrambling things, so the letters of mass are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
hup is a call to a horse to turn to the right

explanation.surface: A disastrous mass swerve to the right follows a car crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catastrophic' scrambles mass. The call to a horse to turn right is old carters' language that few solvers will know. 'after' only links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash-up is a violent collision, so it is another word for a crash.

clue.text: Could Cockney sound grand?

annotationWithheld.why: Could Cockney sound grand? (6): the parse needs Cockney 'might 'e' for 'might he', but no clue word supplies 'he'; Could gives only MIGHT, so the final Y has no source

clue.text: In charge of opening up the polar regions?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a space is an opening or gap

explanation.surface: Someone in authority is opening up the Arctic and Antarctic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening up' reads as exploring, but 'up' reverses SPACE in this down entry; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice caps cover the land at the poles, so the polar regions are described by what covers them, hence the question mark.

clue.text: House originally insisted no one supports voting for the masses

indicators.note: in a down entry a piece that supports another sits beneath it
originally points to the first letter of insisted

parts.note: a poll is a vote
O is the figure nought, used for no
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The House said nobody backs giving ordinary people the vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supports' places O and I below POLL in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoi polloi, Greek for the many, is used in English for ordinary people, so it means the masses.

clue.text: When the old French actress first stripped off?

parts.note: ye is an old form of the

indicators.note: the first letter is stripped away from the word

parts.note: Brigitte Bardot is the famous French actress

explanation.surface: When did the ageing French film star first take her clothes off?
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped off' suggests a nude scene, fitting Bardot's image, but it removes the B from BARDOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The year dot is an informal phrase for a time long ago, so it answers the question when, as a time.

clue.text: Gunners put French international up front where there's lots of empty space

definitions.text: where there's lots of empty space

indicators.note: placed up front means set at the head, so this piece comes before the other

parts.note: Louis Saha was a French international footballer
RA, the Royal Artillery, are the gunners

explanation.surface: Arsenal, the Gunners, play a French international up front and leave lots of space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gunners' is Arsenal's nickname, suggesting football, but here it is the Royal Artillery, RA; 'put' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sahara is a vast desert, so it is a place with great stretches of empty land.

clue.text: Corrupt CIA men ran cartel from Nicaragua, perhaps

indicators.note: corrupt as a verb means to spoil or twist, so the letters of the following words are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: American intelligence agents run a drug cartel from Central America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' reads as a verb ordering the CIA men about, but it signals that CIAMENRANCARTEL is to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicaragua is one country of the Central American isthmus, so its people are an example, marked by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Start to bedizen jumper with chain and ornamental clasp

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, here the first of bedizen

parts.note: a roo, short for kangaroo, is a famous jumper
CH is the abbreviation for chain, an old unit of length

explanation.surface: Begin decorating a sweater with a chain and a fancy fastening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jumper' suggests a British sweater, but it is the kangaroo; 'chain' is the surveyors' length of 22 yards, abbreviated CH.
explanation.definitionFit: A brooch is a decorative pin fastened onto clothing, so an ornamental clasp describes it directly.

clue.text: Canada used to provide habitat for one short snake

indicators.note: giving a home to something means holding it inside, so one piece sits within another
used in the sense of worked over or knocked about, so the letters of Canada are rearranged
short means cut off before the end, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: one written out as a word

explanation.surface: Canada once offered a home to a single undersized snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used' scrambles the country into ANACDA, and 'to provide habitat for' means the shortened word goes into it after the fourth letter. 'snake' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The anaconda is a very large South American constrictor, one kind of snake.

clue.text: Delightful fruit tree almost in bloom

parts.note: sweet can mean charming or delightful

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a pear is a common fruit tree

explanation.surface: A lovely orchard tree is very nearly in flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' only links to the definition; 'bloom' means a flower, not a blush.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a fragrant climbing garden flower, so a bloom names it by category.

clue.text: In possession of mescal, a torturous way of getting high

indicators.note: being in possession of means holding, so the answer is held within these words

explanation.surface: Having some mescal is a painful route to intoxication.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting high' suggests the drug mescal, but the answer rises between floors: mESCAL A TORturous.
explanation.definitionFit: An escalator is a moving staircase, which carries people up to a higher level.

clue.text: Gunshots from a drab outlying part of London

indicators.note: lying around the outside means one piece encloses the other

parts.note: drab is an old word for a slovenly woman, a slut
taken as written
E is the East London postal district

explanation.surface: Gunfire is heard from a dreary district on the edge of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drab' looks like an adjective but is the old noun for a slattern; 'outlying' puts SLUT around A, and E is London's East postal area.
explanation.definitionFit: A salute can be a ceremonial firing of guns, so gunshots fired in honour describe it.

clue.text: Gutless FSA must ultimately tackle wealthy banker, for example

indicators.note: gutless means with the insides removed, leaving only the outer letters
ultimately points to the final letter of must

parts.note: a cat is a nautical tackle used for hoisting an anchor

explanation.surface: The spineless Financial Services Authority must finally take on a rich banker.
explanation.walkthrough: The FSA was Britain's financial regulator. 'tackle' looks like a verb but is the noun: a cat is a ship's hoisting tackle.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat cat is a slang term for a rich, privileged person, and a highly paid banker is a typical example.

clue.text: Alternative stock market's not so unpredictable

parts.note: AIM is the London Alternative Investment Market
less means to a smaller degree, not so much

explanation.surface: The smaller-company stock market is not as volatile as it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: AIM is the London Stock Exchange's market for smaller companies; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aimless means without direction or purpose, so random and unpredictable.

clue.text: Perhaps Fourth Programme — a long-standing BBC production

definitions.meaning: fourth gear in a car may be the highest one available, marked by perhaps
the BBC motoring show running since 1977

explanation.surface: A radio channel called the Fourth Programme might be a long-running BBC show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fourth Programme' recalls BBC radio's old Home and Third Programmes, but fourth is a car gear.
explanation.definitionFit: In a four-speed gearbox fourth is the highest ratio, and the motoring programme of that name is a long-running BBC show.

clue.text: Shami at Liberty pens letter to provoke leaders

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so one piece is written inside the other
at liberty means set free, so the letters of Shami are loosed and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
ess is the spelt-out name of the letter S

explanation.surface: Shami Chakrabarti of the campaign group Liberty writes a letter to stir up those in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Shami Chakrabarti ran the British civil-liberties group Liberty, so 'at Liberty' looks like her job title; here it rearranges her name to MIAHS. 'to provoke' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Messiahs are saviours or charismatic figures whom people follow, hence leaders.

clue.text: High points following cross misunderstandings

indicators.note: following means coming after, so one piece goes after the other

parts.note: to cross breeds is to mix them
ups are good times or high points

explanation.surface: Peaks of success come after an angry confrontation of confusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Mix-ups are confusions where things are mistaken for one another, so misunderstandings.

clue.text: Secretly felling a tree

indicators.note: felling a tree turns it on its side, so the word is turned around

parts.note: Sorbus is the genus of trees including the rowan
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cuts down a tree without anyone knowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'felling' gives SUBROS. Sorbus is the botanical genus of the rowan and whitebeam, a name few solvers know.
explanation.definitionFit: Sub rosa is Latin for under the rose, a symbol of confidentiality, so it means in secret.

clue.text: It protects one's thatch from the rain storm

indicators.note: storm suggests violent upheaval, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something shields your hair from a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thatch' is slang for a head of hair; 'from' is a link before the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairnet is a fine mesh worn to keep the hair in place, so it protects a person's hair.

clue.text: Little prince gets animal virus

parts.note: small is a synonym of little
an ox is a farm animal

explanation.surface: A young prince catches a disease passed on from livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: Smallpox is a disease caused by the variola virus, so the illness is named by its cause.

clue.text: VIP initially bet £1,000 and won £1,000

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of bet

parts.note: one grand, written as I for one and G for grand, a thousand pounds
W is the abbreviation for won in sports results tables
again one grand: I for one and G for grand

explanation.surface: An important gambler first stakes a thousand pounds and wins a thousand back.
explanation.walkthrough: G for grand (a thousand pounds) is a crossword staple; here each £1,000 is read as 1 G, the 1 becoming the Roman I.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigwig is an informal term for an important person, just as VIP abbreviates very important person.

clue.text: Assistant making sportsman lose weight

indicators.note: to lose something is to have it taken away, so the letter is removed

parts.note: a golfer is a sportsman
L stands for pound, the weight, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A helper turns a player into a slimmer one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lose weight' sounds like dieting, but it removes L (pound) from GOLFER; 'making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A gofer is a junior who runs errands, so an assistant, from go for.

clue.text: Protection from the elements when poor frigate founders

indicators.note: a ship that founders sinks and breaks up, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship needs shelter from the storm when a weak frigate goes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'founders' reads as the sinking of the frigate but signals that WHENPOORFRIGATE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Weatherproofing is treatment that keeps out wind and rain, so it gives protection against the weather.

clue.text: Writer's art really captivated philosopher

indicators.note: captivated means held captive, so the answer is held within these clue words

explanation.surface: A writer's skill truly enthralled a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivated' looks like praise but means the run is held inside: writer'S ART REally.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre was the French existentialist philosopher, so he is an example of a philosopher.

clue.text: Incentive to swap rubbish vehicle

indicators.note: swap tells us to exchange the order of the two pieces as they appear in the clue

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A reason to trade in an old banger of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swap' does the work: the clue names rubbish first and vehicle second, and the answer takes them the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrot, as in carrot and stick, is a reward dangled to encourage someone, an idiomatic incentive.
